On pp-Adic Valuation Trees Arising from Laplace Transform of Fibonacci Polynomials

Rigoberto Flórez Address: Department of Mathematics and Data Analytics
The Citadel
Charleston, SC
U.S.A. Email address: rflorez1@citadel.edu , Robinson Higuita-Diaz Address: Escuela de Matemáticas y Estadística, Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia, Tunja, Colombia. Email address: robinson.higuita@uptc.edu.co and José L. Ramírez Address: Departamento de Matemáticas, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Bogotá, Colombia. Email address: jlramirezr@unal.edu.co
Date: October 27, 2026
Abstract.

We study the pp-adic valuation trees associated with the sequence

en=∫0∞e−t​Fn​(t)​𝑑t,e_{n}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}F_{n}(t)\,dt,

obtained by evaluating the Laplace transforms of the Fibonacci polynomials at 11. We answer an open question of Givens and Moll in the negative by constructing an explicit counterexample showing that even internal branches need not be simple. We then reformulate the Givens–Moll lifting criteria for the even and odd subsequences in terms of the roots and derivatives of two associated polynomials. In particular, simple roots modulo pp give rise to simple internal branches. Finally, we develop a recursive lifting procedure that determines the unique surviving residue class at each level of a branch associated with a simple root and computes the pp-adic valuations of the corresponding terms.

Key words and phrases: 
Fibonacci sequence, pp-adic valuation, valuation tree.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11B39, 11B50, 11B75.

Dedicated to the memory of our friend and colleague Florian Luca.11 1 Florian Luca had agreed to collaborate with us on this series of papers, but, unexpectedly, he passed away before he had the opportunity to communicate any results of his work to us. Although we were unable to pursue this endeavor with him, we remember with profound gratitude his friendship, generosity, encouragement, and the inspiration he provided. This paper is dedicated to his memory.

1. Introduction

Givens and Moll [5] studied the sequence obtained by evaluating the Laplace transforms of the Fibonacci polynomials at 11. More recently, Flórez, Higuita, and Ramírez [4] extended this construction to other families of polynomials satisfying second-order recurrences, including the Lucas, Fermat, Morgan–Voyce, and Vieta polynomials.

Let Fn​(x)F_{n}(x) denote the nnth Fibonacci polynomial, defined by

Fn​(x)=x​Fn−1​(x)+Fn−2​(x),n≥2,F_{n}(x)=xF_{n-1}(x)+F_{n-2}(x),\qquad n\geq 2,

with initial conditions F0​(x)=0F_{0}(x)=0 and F1​(x)=1F_{1}(x)=1. Givens and Moll considered the integer sequence (en)n≥1(e_{n})_{n\geq 1} defined by

en=∫0∞e−t​Fn​(t)​𝑑t.e_{n}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}F_{n}(t)\,dt.

We refer to this sequence as the FiboLaplace sequence. Its first terms are

1, 1, 3, 8, 31, 147, 853, 5824, 45741, 405845, 4012711, 43733976,….1,\ 1,\ 3,\ 8,\ 31,\ 147,\ 853,\ 5824,\ 45741,\ 405845,\ 4012711,\ 43733976,\ldots.

It appears in the OEIS as [7, A003470]

The FiboLaplace sequence admits the explicit representation

en=∑i=0⌊(n−1)/2⌋(n−i−1)!i!,n≥1,e_{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}\frac{(n-i-1)!}{i!},\qquad n\geq 1, (1.1)

and satisfies the nonhomogeneous recurrence

em=(m−1)​em−1−em−2+1−(−1)m,m≥3,e_{m}=(m-1)e_{m-1}-e_{m-2}+1-(-1)^{m},\qquad m\geq 3, (1.2)

with initial conditions e1=e2=1e_{1}=e_{2}=1. Further properties and generalizations of this sequence can be found in [4, 5].

A central topic in [5] is the study of the pp-adic valuation of the terms of the FiboLaplace sequence. For a prime pp, recall that νp​(m)\nu_{p}(m) denotes the largest nonnegative integer rr such that pr|mp^{r}\mid m. For example, Givens and Moll obtained the following complete description of the 33-adic valuation of ene_{n}:

ν3​(en)={ν3​(n),if ​n≡0(mod6),0,if ​n≡1,2,4,5(mod6),1,if ​n≡3(mod6).\nu_{3}(e_{n})=\begin{cases}\nu_{3}(n),&\text{if }n\equiv 0\pmod{6},\\[2.84526pt] 0,&\text{if }n\equiv 1,2,4,5\pmod{6},\\[2.84526pt] 1,&\text{if }n\equiv 3\pmod{6}.\end{cases} (1.3)

Valuation trees have been used to study the pp-adic valuations of integer sequences; see, for instance, [6]. Examples include Stirling numbers of the second kind [2], truncated exponential sums [1], Eulerian numbers [3], and a sequence arising from a rational integral [8]. Givens and Moll [5] constructed a tree structure for the FiboLaplace sequence that organizes the congruence classes of indices according to the pp-adic valuations of the corresponding terms. A vertex of such a tree represents a congruence class of indices. It is called terminal when the valuation is constant on that class and nonterminal when further refinement is required. An internal branch is called simple when every level contains exactly one nonterminal vertex. For even indices, Givens and Moll established a lifting criterion that guarantees the simplicity of an internal branch. They subsequently asked whether every even internal branch must be simple.

The first objective of this paper is to answer this question. We show that the answer is negative by giving an explicit counterexample for p=971p=971. We also observe that the analogous statement for odd internal branches already fails for p=3p=3.

Our second objective is to provide an algebraic interpretation of the lifting criteria of Givens and Moll. We associate polynomials 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) and 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) with the even and odd subsequences, respectively. Their roots modulo pp correspond to the internal roots of the associated valuation trees. Thus, the nonvanishing conditions in the Givens–Moll criteria are equivalent to the corresponding roots being simple modulo pp. It follows that a simple root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) or 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) gives rise to a simple even or odd internal branch, respectively.

Finally, we use the lifting congruences constructively. Along a simple branch, they determine the unique surviving residue class at each successive level and therefore provide a recursive method for computing the corresponding pp-adic valuations. We illustrate this procedure in detail for p=13p=13, where the four even internal branches are simple and their successive surviving residues can be computed one base-1313 digit at a time.

We first introduce the pp-adic valuation trees associated with the FiboLaplace sequence and illustrate their structure through the case p=13p=13. After recalling the lifting criteria of Givens and Moll, we present a counterexample for p=971p=971 and then give an algebraic interpretation of the even and odd criteria in terms of the polynomials 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) and 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x). This interpretation leads to simple-root criteria and a partial converse. We conclude by developing a recursive procedure for following simple branches and computing the corresponding pp-adic valuations, with a detailed illustration for p=13p=13.

2. Discussion on the Question of Givens and Moll

In this section, we introduce the background needed to study the question of Givens and Moll [5] concerning the pp-adic valuations of the FiboLaplace sequence (en)n≥1(e_{n})_{n\geq 1}. For a prime pp and a positive integer mm, the pp-adic valuation of mm, denoted by νp​(m)\nu_{p}(m), is the largest nonnegative integer rr such that pr|mp^{r}\mid m. Thus, νp​(m)\nu_{p}(m) is the exponent of pp in the prime factorization of mm. For example,

ν2​(100)=ν2​(22⋅52)=2andν7​(100)=0.\nu_{2}(100)=\nu_{2}(2^{2}\cdot 5^{2})=2\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nu_{7}(100)=0.

To motivate the construction of the associated valuation trees, we begin with the case p=13p=13. Figure 1 displays the values of ν13​(en)\nu_{13}(e_{n}) for 1≤n≤2001\leq n\leq 200. Even in this relatively short range, a pattern is apparent: positive valuations occur at regularly spaced indices, and at some of these indices the valuation is greater than 11.

The first of these regularities is explained by a result of Givens and Moll [5]. They proved that, for every positive integer MM, the sequence (enmodM)n≥1(e_{n}\bmod M)_{n\geq 1} is periodic with period 2​M2M. In particular,

en+26≡en(mod13).e_{n+26}\equiv e_{n}\pmod{13}.

Consequently,

13∣en⟺13∣en+26.13\mid e_{n}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 13\mid e_{n+26}.

Thus divisibility by 1313 depends only on the residue class of nn modulo 2626. Figure 2 displays the residues enmod13e_{n}\bmod 13 for 1≤n≤2001\leq n\leq 200. The dashed vertical lines are spaced 2626 units apart, making the periodicity particularly easy to see.

This suggests that we first divide the positive integers into the classes

I13​(r)={n≥1:n≡r(mod26)},1≤r≤26.I_{13}(r)=\{n\geq 1:n\equiv r\pmod{26}\},\qquad 1\leq r\leq 26.

A computation over one period gives

13∣er⟺r∈{8,12,14,18,26}.13\mid e_{r}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad r\in\{8,12,14,18,26\}.

It follows immediately from periodicity that ν13​(en)=0\nu_{13}(e_{n})=0 for every nn outside the five classes

I13​(8)\displaystyle I_{13}(8) ={8,34,60,86,112,138,164,190,…},\displaystyle=\{8,34,60,86,112,138,164,190,\dots\},
I13​(12)\displaystyle I_{13}(12) ={12,38,64,90,116,142,168,194,…},\displaystyle=\{12,38,64,90,116,142,168,194,\dots\},
I13​(14)\displaystyle I_{13}(14) ={14,40,66,92,118,144,170,196,…},\displaystyle=\{14,40,66,92,118,144,170,196,\dots\},
I13​(18)\displaystyle I_{13}(18) ={18,44,70,96,122,148,174,200,…},\displaystyle=\{18,44,70,96,122,148,174,200,\dots\},
I13​(26)\displaystyle I_{13}(26) ={26,52,78,104,130,156,182,208,…}.\displaystyle=\{26,52,78,104,130,156,182,208,\dots\}.

One might initially expect the residue class of nn modulo 2626 to determine not only whether 13|en13\mid e_{n}, but also the exact value of ν13​(en)\nu_{13}(e_{n}). However, this is not the case. For example,

8≡34(mod26),8\equiv 34\pmod{26},

whereas

ν13​(e8)=1andν13​(e34)=2.\nu_{13}(e_{8})=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nu_{13}(e_{34})=2.

Thus, the residue class of nn modulo 2626 determines whether ν13​(en)>0\nu_{13}(e_{n})>0, but not its exact value. In particular, it does not distinguish between indices for which the valuation is 11, 22, or higher. This leads naturally to the following question:

What additional information is needed to distinguish the valuations within a class I13​(r)I_{13}(r)?

To detect whether ν13​(en)≥2\nu_{13}(e_{n})\geq 2, we must refine the congruence classes modulo 2626. By the periodicity theorem applied with M=132M=13^{2}, the sequence

(enmod132)n≥1\bigl(e_{n}\bmod 13^{2}\bigr)_{n\geq 1}

has period

2⋅132=338.2\cdot 13^{2}=338.

It is therefore natural to refine each residue class modulo 2626 into residue classes modulo 338338.

Hence a residue class modulo 2626 breaks into 1313 residue classes modulo 338338. For example,

I13​(8)=⋃j=012{n≥1:n≡8+26​j(mod338)}.I_{13}(8)=\bigcup_{j=0}^{12}\left\{n\geq 1:n\equiv 8+26j\pmod{338}\right\}.

Thus the class n≡8(mod26)n\equiv 8\pmod{26} is refined into

n≡8, 34, 60, 86, 112, 138, 164, 190, 216, 242, 268, 294, 320(mod338).n\equiv 8,\ 34,\ 60,\ 86,\ 112,\ 138,\ 164,\ 190,\ 216,\ 242,\ 268,\ 294,\ 320\pmod{338}.

A computation modulo 13213^{2} now reveals something more interesting. Twelve of these classes contain only indices nn for which ν13​(en)=1\nu_{13}(e_{n})=1, whereas the class n≡34(mod338)n\equiv 34\pmod{338} satisfies ν13​(en)≥2\nu_{13}(e_{n})\geq 2. Thus, the original class I13​(8)I_{13}(8) has exactly one subclass in which the valuation can increase.

This refinement is naturally represented by a tree, which we denote by T13​(8)T_{13}(8). The root corresponds to the residue class n≡8(mod26)n\equiv 8\pmod{26}. Its 1313 children, denoted by v1,0,v1,1,…,v1,12v_{1,0},v_{1,1},\ldots,v_{1,12}, correspond respectively to the classes

n≡8+26​j(mod338),0≤j≤12.n\equiv 8+26j\pmod{338},\qquad 0\leq j\leq 12.

We place the value 11 at a vertex when every index in the corresponding class has 1313-adic valuation exactly 11. If the valuation may be larger, we write instead a lower bound. In the present example, v1,1v_{1,1} is the unique vertex labeled ≥2\geq 2, since it represents the class

n≡34(mod338).n\equiv 34\pmod{338}.

The other twelve vertices are terminal at this stage.

We now repeat the same procedure on the unique class that survives. Since the sequence modulo 13313^{3} has period 2⋅133=43942\cdot 13^{3}=4394, the class n≡34(mod338)n\equiv 34\pmod{338} splits into the 1313 classes

n≡34+338​j(mod4394),0≤j≤12.n\equiv 34+338j\pmod{4394},\qquad 0\leq j\leq 12.

These form the second generation v2,0,v2,1,…,v2,12v_{2,0},v_{2,1},\ldots,v_{2,12} of the tree. Again, twelve classes have constant valuation 22, while exactly one continues 34+338=37234+338=372. Thus v2,1v_{2,1} represents

n≡372(mod4394)n\equiv 372\pmod{4394}

and is labeled ≥3\geq 3.

The refinement process may be continued inductively. At each step, a surviving congruence class modulo 2⋅13k2\cdot 13^{k} is refined into 1313 congruence classes modulo 2⋅13k+12\cdot 13^{k+1}. A vertex becomes terminal once the exact valuation is determined. In contrast, a vertex labeled by a lower bound, for example ν13​(en)≥k+1\nu_{13}(e_{n})\geq k+1, must be refined at the next level. Figure 3 shows the first several levels of the tree T13​(8)T_{13}(8).

The tree T13​(8)T_{13}(8) is not an isolated phenomenon. The class I13​(12)I_{13}(12) behaves in exactly the same way. At the first refinement, twelve of its children have valuation 11, while a unique child has valuation at least 22:

12(mod26)⟶38(mod338).12\pmod{26}\quad\longrightarrow\quad 38\pmod{338}.

The classes I13​(14)I_{13}(14) and I13​(18)I_{13}(18) exhibit the same behavior, although their surviving children occur at a different position:

14(mod26)⟶300(mod338),14\pmod{26}\quad\longrightarrow\quad 300\pmod{338},

and

18(mod26)⟶304(mod338).18\pmod{26}\quad\longrightarrow\quad 304\pmod{338}.

Finally, the remaining class I13​(26)I_{13}(26) also has a unique surviving child:

26(mod26)⟶338(mod338).26\pmod{26}\quad\longrightarrow\quad 338\pmod{338}.

There is also a striking symmetry among the four nonzero residue classes. Indeed,

8+18=26,12+14=26,8+18=26,\qquad 12+14=26,

and the corresponding surviving residues at the next level satisfy

34+304=338,38+300=338.34+304=338,\qquad 38+300=338.

Thus the pairs T13​(8)T_{13}(8) and T13​(18)T_{13}(18), and T13​(12)T_{13}(12) and T13​(14)T_{13}(14), already appear to be related by reflection.

The example p=13p=13 therefore suggests a remarkably simple branching pattern. Each relevant residue class modulo 2626 splits into 1313 children at the next level. Of these children, twelve have their valuations completely determined and become terminal, while exactly one continues to a higher valuation. This same structure is visible at the successive levels of T13​(8)T_{13}(8), as shown in Figure 3.

The example p=13p=13 leads us to ask whether this branching pattern persists for other primes and whether the unique surviving child, when it exists, can be determined without computing the often very large terms ene_{n} directly.

Motivated by these questions, we now formalize the refinement process described above through the notion of a pp-adic valuation tree. For an odd prime pp, a residue rr, and k≥0k\geq 0, let

Ip,k​(r)={n≥1:n≡r(mod2​pk+1)}.I_{p,k}(r)=\{n\geq 1:n\equiv r\pmod{2p^{k+1}}\}.

Thus, the classes considered in our example are I13​(8)=I13,0​(8)I_{13}(8)=I_{13,0}(8), and its first refinement consists of the 1313 classes

I13,1​(8+26​j),0≤j≤12.I_{13,1}(8+26j),\qquad 0\leq j\leq 12.

More generally, every class Ip,k​(r)I_{p,k}(r) decomposes as

Ip,k​(r)=⋃j=0p−1Ip,k+1​(r+2​pk+1​j).I_{p,k}(r)=\bigcup_{j=0}^{p-1}I_{p,k+1}\bigl(r+2p^{k+1}j\bigr).

This elementary refinement is the underlying structure of the valuation trees.

Definition 2.1.

Let pp be an odd prime and let rr satisfy p|erp\mid e_{r}. The pp-adic valuation tree rooted at rr, denoted by Tp​(r)T_{p}(r), is defined recursively as follows.

The root represents the class Ip,0​(r)I_{p,0}(r), and each vertex at level kk represents a congruence class Ip,k​(a)I_{p,k}(a). Such a vertex is called terminal if νp​(en)\nu_{p}(e_{n}) is constant as n∈Ip,k​(a)n\in I_{p,k}(a); otherwise, it is called nonterminal.

Each nonterminal vertex representing Ip,k​(a)I_{p,k}(a) has pp children, corresponding to the classes

Ip,k+1​(a+2​pk+1​j),0≤j≤p−1.I_{p,k+1}\bigl(a+2p^{k+1}j\bigr),\qquad 0\leq j\leq p-1.

Terminal vertices are not refined further.

The tree constructed in Figure 3 is precisely T13​(8)T_{13}(8). Its root represents I13,0​(8)I_{13,0}(8), and its first generation consists of the classes

I13,1​(8+26​j),0≤j≤12.I_{13,1}(8+26j),\qquad 0\leq j\leq 12.

The unique nonterminal vertex at this level corresponds to j=1j=1, that is, to the class I13,1​(34)I_{13,1}(34).

Among the roots modulo 2​p2p, the class 2​p(mod2​p)2p\pmod{2p} plays a distinguished role. Following Givens and Moll, a root r∈{1,…,2​p−1}r\in\{1,\ldots,2p-1\} for which p|erp\mid e_{r} is called an internal root, and the corresponding tree Tp​(r)T_{p}(r) is called an internal branch. Thus, for p=13p=13, the roots 88, 1212, 1414, and 1818 are internal, whereas 26=2​p26=2p is the distinguished root.

Definition 2.2.

An internal branch Tp​(r)T_{p}(r) is called simple if every level contains exactly one nonterminal vertex.

In particular, an internal root that is already terminal does not define a simple branch. The computations above suggest that the internal branches T13​(8)T_{13}(8), T13​(12)T_{13}(12), T13​(14)T_{13}(14), and T13​(18)T_{13}(18) are simple. Givens and Moll introduced a difference function that not only proves this fact, but also explains why exactly one child survives at each level.

2.1. The lifting criterion of Givens and Moll

We now recall the lifting criterion of Givens and Moll, which provides a sufficient condition for an internal branch to be simple and determines the unique child on which the valuation may increase.

For n≥1n\geq 1 and j≥0j\geq 0, define

P⁡(n,j)={1,j=0,∏ℓ=1j(n2−ℓ2),j≥1.P(n,j)=\begin{cases}1,&j=0,\\[2.84526pt] \displaystyle\prod_{\ell=1}^{j}(n^{2}-\ell^{2}),&j\geq 1.\end{cases} (2.1)

Givens and Moll showed that the even-indexed terms of the FiboLaplace sequence satisfy

e2​n=n​∑j=0n−1P⁡(n,j).e_{2n}=n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}P(n,j).

Accordingly, we define

A⁡(n)=e2​nn=∑j=0n−1P⁡(n,j).A(n)=\frac{e_{2n}}{n}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}P(n,j). (2.2)

Let pp be an odd prime. For r≥1r\geq 1, define

Δp​(n,j,r)≡P⁡(n+pr,j)−P⁡(n,j)pr(modp)\Delta_{p}(n,j;r)\equiv\frac{P(n+p^{r},j)-P(n,j)}{p^{r}}\pmod{p} (2.3)

and

δp​(n)≡∑j=0pΔp​(n,j,r)(modp).\delta_{p}(n)\equiv\sum_{j=0}^{p}\Delta_{p}(n,j;r)\pmod{p}. (2.4)

The quantity δp​(n)\delta_{p}(n) is independent of rr. The following result combines [5, Lemma 4.8 and Theorem 4.12].

Theorem 2.3 (Givens and Moll).

Let pp be an odd prime.

  1. (1)

    For all integers n,r≥1n,r\geq 1 and j≥0j\geq 0,

    A⁡(n+j​pr)−A⁡(n)≡j​δp​(n)​pr(modpr+1).A(n+jp^{r})-A(n)\equiv j\delta_{p}(n)p^{r}\pmod{p^{r+1}}. (2.5)
  2. (2)

    Let a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\} satisfy p|e2​ap\mid e_{2a}. If

    δp​(a)≢0(modp),\delta_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p},

    then the internal branch Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) is simple; that is, every level contains exactly one nonterminal vertex.

To explain how the lifting congruence determines the children of a vertex, suppose that a nonterminal vertex at level r−1r-1 is represented, in half-index notation, by a class n(modpr)n\pmod{p^{r}}, where n≡a(modp)n\equiv a\pmod{p}. Write

A⁡(n)≡c​pr(modpr+1).A(n)\equiv cp^{r}\pmod{p^{r+1}}.

Since a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}, we have p∤np\nmid n. Therefore, A⁡(n)A(n) and e2​n=n​A​(n)e_{2n}=nA(n) have the same pp-adic valuation.

The pp children of this vertex are represented by

n+j​pr,j=0,1,…,p−1.n+jp^{r},\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,p-1.

Dividing (2.5) by prp^{r} gives

A⁡(n+j​pr)pr≡c+j​δp​(n)(modp).\frac{A(n+jp^{r})}{p^{r}}\equiv c+j\delta_{p}(n)\pmod{p}. (2.6)

If δp​(n)≢0(modp)\delta_{p}(n)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, the linear congruence

c+j​δp​(n)≡0(modp)c+j\delta_{p}(n)\equiv 0\pmod{p}

has a unique solution jj modulo pp. Consequently, exactly one child has valuation at least r+1r+1. On each of the remaining p−1p-1 child classes, the valuation is constantly equal to rr, by periodicity modulo pr+1p^{r+1}, these children are terminal. Repeating this argument at each successive nonterminal vertex shows that Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) is simple.

We now return to the example p=13p=13. The internal root 88 corresponds to the half-index a=4a=4. Since

A⁡(4)=e84=1456=13⋅112,A(4)=\frac{e_{8}}{4}=1456=13\cdot 112,

we have c≡112≡8(mod13)c\equiv 112\equiv 8\pmod{13}. Moreover,

δ13​(4)≡5(mod13).\delta_{13}(4)\equiv 5\pmod{13}.

The first surviving child is therefore determined by

8+5​j≡0(mod13).8+5j\equiv 0\pmod{13}.

The unique solution is j=1j=1, giving the full index 2​(4+13)=342(4+13)=34. Thus the branch begins

8(mod26)⟶34(mod338),8\pmod{26}\longrightarrow 34\pmod{338},

as shown in Figure 3.

The remaining three internal roots correspond to the half-indices 66, 77, and 99, for which

δ13​(6)≡11,δ13​(7)≡2,δ13​(9)≡8(mod13).\delta_{13}(6)\equiv 11,\qquad\delta_{13}(7)\equiv 2,\qquad\delta_{13}(9)\equiv 8\pmod{13}.

Together with δ13​(4)≡5(mod13)\delta_{13}(4)\equiv 5\pmod{13}, these values are all nonzero. Therefore, Theorem 2.3 proves that the four internal branches rooted at 88, 1212, 1414, and 1818 are simple.

Givens and Moll also obtained a parallel lifting criterion for the odd subsequence; see [5, Example 4.14]. Set

B⁡(n)=e2​n+1=1+∑j=1nn⁡(n+j)​P​(n,j−1),n≥0.B(n)=e_{2n+1}=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n}n(n+j)P(n,j-1),\qquad n\geq 0. (2.7)

For r≥1r\geq 1, define

δp′​(n)≡B⁡(n+pr)−B⁡(n)pr(modp).\delta^{\prime}_{p}(n)\equiv\frac{B(n+p^{r})-B(n)}{p^{r}}\pmod{p}. (2.8)

The quotient is an integer, and its residue modulo pp is independent of rr.

Theorem 2.4 (Givens and Moll).

Let pp be an odd prime.

  1. (1)

    For all integers n≥0n\geq 0, r≥1r\geq 1, and j≥0j\geq 0,

    B⁡(n+j​pr)−B⁡(n)≡j​δp′​(n)​pr(modpr+1).B(n+jp^{r})-B(n)\equiv j\delta^{\prime}_{p}(n)p^{r}\pmod{p^{r+1}}. (2.9)
  2. (2)

    Let a∈{0,1,…,p−1}a\in\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\} satisfy p|e2​a+1p\mid e_{2a+1}. If

    δp′​(a)≢0(modp),\delta^{\prime}_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p},

    then the internal branch Tp​(2​a+1)T_{p}(2a+1) is simple.

The preceding results led Givens and Moll to ask whether every even internal branch must be simple.

Open problem 1 (Givens and Moll).

Let pp be an odd prime and let a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\} satisfy p|e2​ap\mid e_{2a}. Must the internal branch Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) be simple?

Theorem 2.3 gives the sufficient condition

δp​(a)≢0(modp)⟹Tp​(2​a)​ is simple.\delta_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_{p}(2a)\text{ is simple}.

This leads naturally to the stronger question of whether this nonvanishing condition holds automatically at every even internal root; that is, whether

p|e2​a⟹δp​(a)≢0(modp).p\mid e_{2a}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\delta_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

It is important to distinguish these two questions. Givens and Moll proved that the nonvanishing of δp​(a)\delta_{p}(a) implies simplicity, but they did not prove the converse. Thus, finding an internal root for which δp​(a)≡0(modp)\delta_{p}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p} would disprove the stronger nonvanishing statement, but would not by itself show that the corresponding branch is not simple.

Our counterexample shows that both assertions fail simultaneously. For a certain even internal root, we have δp​(a)≡0(modp)\delta_{p}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}, and the root itself is terminal. Consequently, the corresponding internal branch is not simple.

3. A Terminal Even Internal Branch

The vanishing of δp​(a)\delta_{p}(a) does not, by itself, imply that the corresponding internal branch is not simple. It only shows that the sufficient criterion of Givens and Moll does not apply. When the initial valuation is exactly one, however, the lifting congruence gives a stronger conclusion: the root is terminal. We use this observation to show that T971​(388)T_{971}(388) is not simple, thereby giving a negative answer to the question of Givens and Moll in the even case. The analogous odd counterexample is more immediate: the valuation formula of Givens and Moll for p=3p=3 shows directly that the branch T3​(3)T_{3}(3) is terminal.

Proposition 3.1.

Let pp be an odd prime and let a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}. If νp​(e2​a)=1\nu_{p}(e_{2a})=1 and δp​(a)≡0(modp)\delta_{p}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}, then the root of the internal branch Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) is terminal. More precisely,

νp​(e2​(a+j​p))=1for every ​j≥0.\nu_{p}\bigl(e_{2(a+jp)}\bigr)=1\qquad\text{for every }j\geq 0. (3.1)
Proof.

Since p∤ap\nmid a, we have νp​(A⁡(a))=νp​(e2​a)=1\nu_{p}(A(a))=\nu_{p}(e_{2a})=1. Taking n=an=a and r=1r=1 in (2.5) gives

A⁡(a+j​p)−A⁡(a)≡j​δp​(a)​p≡0(modp2).A(a+jp)-A(a)\equiv j\delta_{p}(a)p\equiv 0\pmod{p^{2}}.

Hence

A⁡(a+j​p)≡A⁡(a)(modp2)A(a+jp)\equiv A(a)\pmod{p^{2}}

for every j≥0j\geq 0. Since A⁡(a)A(a) is divisible by pp but not by p2p^{2}, the same is true of A⁡(a+j​p)A(a+jp). Moreover, p∤a+j​pp\nmid a+jp, and therefore νp​(e2​(a+j​p))=1\nu_{p}\bigl(e_{2(a+jp)}\bigr)=1 for every j≥0j\geq 0. Thus the valuation is constant on the root class 2​a(mod2​p)2a\pmod{2p}, so the root is terminal. ∎

3.1. A terminal branch for p=971p=971

We now apply the preceding criterion to construct an even internal branch whose root is terminal. This provides the counterexample needed to answer the question of Givens and Moll negatively.

The following counterexample was discovered through a computer search implemented in Mathematica.

The prime p=971p=971 provides precisely such a situation. For a=194a=194, exact modular computations give

e388≡473848=971⋅488(mod9712)e_{388}\equiv 473848=971\cdot 488\pmod{971^{2}} (3.2)

and

δ971​(194)≡0(mod971).\delta_{971}(194)\equiv 0\pmod{971}. (3.3)

Both congruences can be verified using modular arithmetic. The first is obtained by iterating the recurrence (1.2) modulo 9712971^{2}, while the second follows from the recurrence for Δp​(n,j,r)\Delta_{p}(n,j;r) established by Givens and Moll. Since 971∤488971\nmid 488, equation (3.2) implies that

ν971​(e388)=1.\nu_{971}(e_{388})=1.

Therefore, Proposition 3.1, together with (3.3), yields

ν971​(e388+1942​j)=1for every ​j≥0.\nu_{971}(e_{388+1942j})=1\qquad\text{for every }j\geq 0.

Thus, the root of the internal branch T971​(388)T_{971}(388) is terminal, so T971​(388)T_{971}(388) is not simple. This provides a negative answer to the question of Givens and Moll.

The natural odd analogue is already false for p=3p=3. Indeed, Givens and Moll proved in [5, Theorem 3.6] that ν3​(em)=1\nu_{3}(e_{m})=1 whenever m≡3(mod6)m\equiv 3\pmod{6}. Hence the odd internal root 33 is terminal, and therefore T3​(3)T_{3}(3) is not simple.

The vanishing of the corresponding lifting parameter can also be seen directly. Since

B⁡(1)=e3=3andB⁡(4)=e9≡3(mod9),B(1)=e_{3}=3\qquad\text{and}\qquad B(4)=e_{9}\equiv 3\pmod{9},

we have

δ3′​(1)≡B⁡(4)−B⁡(1)3≡0(mod3).\delta^{\prime}_{3}(1)\equiv\frac{B(4)-B(1)}{3}\equiv 0\pmod{3}.

Thus both the tree question and the stronger nonvanishing question have negative answers in the odd case.

4. A polynomial reformulation of the Givens–Moll criterion

The counterexamples in the preceding section show that the nonvanishing conditions in the Givens–Moll lifting criteria are not automatic at internal roots. We now interpret these conditions algebraically by associating polynomials 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) and 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) with the even and odd subsequences. We show that internal roots correspond to roots of these polynomials modulo pp, while the lifting parameters correspond to their derivatives. This yields simple-root criteria for the simplicity of even and odd internal branches. We also analyze multiple roots and establish, when the initial pp-adic valuation is one, a partial converse in the even case.

4.1. The even polynomial reformulation

We begin with the even subsequence. We introduce a polynomial 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) whose nonzero zeros modulo pp correspond precisely to the even internal root vertices of the valuation tree. We then show that the derivative of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) determines the even lifting parameter δp​(a)\delta_{p}(a). This interpretation yields a criterion for the simplicity of even internal branches in terms of simple zeros of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) and clarifies the behavior when the corresponding zero is multiple.

For each k≥0k\geq 0, the expression P⁡(n,k)P(n,k) in (2.1) is a polynomial in nn. We then define

𝒫p​(x)=∑k=0p−1P⁡(x,k)=1+∑k=1p−1∏ℓ=1k(x2−ℓ2).\mathcal{P}_{p}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}P(x,k)=1+\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\prod_{\ell=1}^{k}(x^{2}-\ell^{2}). (4.1)

For a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}, the terms P⁡(a,k)P(a,k) vanish for k≥ak\geq a. Hence A​(a)=𝒫p​(a)A(a)=\mathcal{P}_{p}(a), and therefore e2​a=a​𝒫p​(a)e_{2a}=a\mathcal{P}_{p}(a). Since p∤ap\nmid a, it follows that

p∣e2​a⟺𝒫p(a)≡0(modp).p\mid e_{2a}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{P}_{p}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

Thus the even internal roots 2​a2a correspond precisely to the nonzero roots aa of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp.

We shall use the following elementary congruence.

Lemma 4.1.

Let f⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x], let pp be a prime, and let r≥1r\geq 1. For all integers aa and jj,

f⁡(a+j​pr)≡f⁡(a)+j​pr​f′​(a)(modpr+1).f(a+jp^{r})\equiv f(a)+jp^{r}f^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p^{r+1}}. (4.2)
Proof.

Write f⁡(x)=∑m=0dcm​xmf(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{d}c_{m}x^{m}. By the binomial theorem,

(a+h)m=∑i=0m(mi)​am−i​hi=am+m​am−1​h+h2​Qm​(a,h),(a+h)^{m}=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}a^{m-i}h^{i}=a^{m}+ma^{m-1}h+h^{2}Q_{m}(a,h),

for some polynomial Qm​(a,h)Q_{m}(a,h) with integer coefficients. Hence

f⁡(a+h)=f⁡(a)+h​f′​(a)+h2​Q​(a,h),f(a+h)=f(a)+hf^{\prime}(a)+h^{2}Q(a,h),

where Q⁡(a,h)Q(a,h) is again a polynomial in aa and hh with integer coefficients. Taking h=j​prh=jp^{r}, the last term is divisible by p2​rp^{2r}, and since r≥1r\geq 1, we have 2​r≥r+12r\geq r+1. Therefore

f⁡(a+j​pr)≡f⁡(a)+j​pr​f′​(a)(modpr+1).∎f(a+jp^{r})\equiv f(a)+jp^{r}f^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p^{r+1}}.\qed

The next result gives the desired interpretation of the quantity δp​(a)\delta_{p}(a).

Theorem 4.2.

Let pp be an odd prime. For every a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\},

δp​(a)≡𝒫p′​(a)(modp).\delta_{p}(a)\equiv\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p}. (4.3)
Proof.

Applying Lemma 4.1 to f⁡(x)=P⁡(x,k)f(x)=P(x,k), with j=1j=1, gives

P⁡(a+pr,k)−P⁡(a,k)≡pr​∂∂x​P​(x,k)|x=a(modpr+1).P(a+p^{r},k)-P(a,k)\equiv p^{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P(x,k)\bigg|_{x=a}\pmod{p^{r+1}}.

Dividing by prp^{r} and using the definition of Δp​(a,k,r)\Delta_{p}(a,k;r) in (2.3), we obtain

Δp​(a,k,r)≡∂∂x​P​(x,k)|x=a(modp).\Delta_{p}(a,k;r)\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P(x,k)\bigg|_{x=a}\pmod{p}.

Therefore, by (2.4),

δp​(a)≡∑k=0p∂∂x​P​(x,k)|x=a(modp)≡𝒫p′​(a)+∂∂x​P​(x,p)|x=a(modp).\delta_{p}(a)\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P(x,k)\bigg|_{x=a}\pmod{p}\equiv\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P(x,p)\bigg|_{x=a}\pmod{p}.

It remains to show that the last term vanishes modulo pp. By the product rule,

∂∂x​P​(x,p)=∑j=1p2​x​∏1≤ℓ≤pℓ≠j(x2−ℓ2).\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P(x,p)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}2x\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell\leq p\\ \ell\neq j\end{subarray}}(x^{2}-\ell^{2}).

Evaluating at x=ax=a, every term with j≠aj\neq a vanishes, since its product contains the factor a2−a2a^{2}-a^{2}. Hence

∂∂x​P​(x,p)|x=a=2​a​∏1≤ℓ≤pℓ≠a(a2−ℓ2).\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P(x,p)\bigg|_{x=a}=2a\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\ell\leq p\\ \ell\neq a\end{subarray}}(a^{2}-\ell^{2}).

Since pp is odd, p−a≠ap-a\neq a, and therefore the factor corresponding to ℓ=p−a\ell=p-a occurs in this product. Moreover, a2−(p−a)2=p⁡(2​a−p)a^{2}-(p-a)^{2}=p(2a-p), so the product is divisible by pp. Thus

∂∂x​P​(x,p)|x=a≡0(modp),\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P(x,p)\bigg|_{x=a}\equiv 0\pmod{p},

and (4.3) follows. ∎

It follows that, whenever 2​a2a is an even internal root, δp​(a)≢0(modp)\delta_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p} if and only if aa is a simple root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp. Thus the stronger nonvanishing question arising from the work of Givens and Moll has the following exact algebraic reformulation:

p|e2​a⟹δp​(a)≢0(modp)for every ​a∈{1,…,p−1}⟺every nonzero root of 𝒫p​(x) modulo p is simple.\begin{split}&p\mid e_{2a}\Longrightarrow\delta_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}\quad\text{for every }a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\\ &\hskip 71.13188pt\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{every nonzero root of $\mathcal{P}_{p}(x)$ modulo $p$ is simple}.\end{split}

This gives the following corrected positive statement.

Theorem 4.3.

Let pp be an odd prime, and let a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\} satisfy p|e2​ap\mid e_{2a}. If aa is a simple root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp, then the internal branch Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) is simple. More precisely, set c≡A⁡(a)p(modp)c\equiv\frac{A(a)}{p}\pmod{p}. Then the unique nonterminal child of the root corresponds to the half-index a+j​pa+jp, where j∈{0,…,p−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\} is the unique solution of

c+j​𝒫p′​(a)≡0(modp).c+j\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}. (4.4)
Proof.

Since aa is a simple root, 𝒫p′​(a)≢0(modp)\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}. By Theorem 4.2, δp​(a)≢0(modp)\delta_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, and Theorem 2.3 therefore implies that Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) is simple.

To determine the first surviving child, take n=an=a and r=1r=1 in (2.5). Dividing by pp gives

A⁡(a+j​p)p≡c+j​δp​(a)≡c+j​𝒫p′​(a)(modp).\frac{A(a+jp)}{p}\equiv c+j\delta_{p}(a)\equiv c+j\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p}.

Since 𝒫p′​(a)≢0(modp)\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, the congruence (4.4) has a unique solution j∈{0,…,p−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}. ∎

Corollary 4.1.

If every nonzero root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp is simple, then every even internal branch of the valuation tree is simple.

Remark 1.

The unique-solution argument in (4.4) is the simple-root case of Hensel lifting. No form of Hensel’s lemma is needed here, however; the lifting congruence (2.5) gives the required conclusion directly.

It remains to understand what the same congruence says when aa is a multiple root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp. Suppose that

A⁡(a)≡c​p(modp2)and𝒫p′​(a)≡0(modp).A(a)\equiv cp\pmod{p^{2}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

Then

A⁡(a+j​p)p≡c(modp)\frac{A(a+jp)}{p}\equiv c\pmod{p}

for every j∈{0,…,p−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}. If c≢0(modp)c\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, then all pp children have valuation exactly 11. Hence the root is terminal. If c≡0(modp)c\equiv 0\pmod{p}, then all pp children have valuation at least 22. In this case, the first-order congruence does not distinguish among them, and higher-order information is needed to determine which children have valuation exactly 22 and which, if any, have higher valuation. Thus multiple roots are precisely the cases in which the first-order Givens–Moll criterion no longer determines a unique surviving child.

4.2. The odd polynomial reformulation

We now develop the corresponding polynomial reformulation for the odd subsequence. We introduce a polynomial 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) whose nonzero roots modulo pp correspond precisely to the odd internal root vertices of the valuation tree. We then show that the derivative of 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) determines the odd lifting parameter δp′​(a)\delta^{\prime}_{p}(a). As in the even case, this interpretation yields a simple-root criterion for the simplicity of odd internal branches and clarifies the behavior when the corresponding polynomial root is multiple.

Set Q⁡(x,0)=1Q(x,0)=1, and for k≥1k\geq 1 define

Q⁡(x,k)=∏ℓ=0k−1(x−ℓ)​(x+ℓ+1).Q(x,k)=\prod_{\ell=0}^{k-1}(x-\ell)(x+\ell+1).

Thus (2.7) can be written as

B⁡(n)=∑k=0nQ⁡(n,k).B(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}Q(n,k).

Define

𝒬p​(x)=∑k=0p−1Q⁡(x,k).\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}Q(x,k). (4.5)

For a∈{0,…,p−1}a\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}, the terms Q⁡(a,k)Q(a,k) vanish for k≥a+1k\geq a+1. Hence B​(a)=𝒬p​(a)B(a)=\mathcal{Q}_{p}(a), and therefore

p∣e2​a+1⟺𝒬p(a)≡0(modp).p\mid e_{2a+1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{Q}_{p}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}. (4.6)

Thus the odd internal roots 2​a+12a+1 correspond precisely to the roots aa of 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) modulo pp.

The odd lifting parameter also has a derivative interpretation.

Proposition 4.4.

For every a∈{0,…,p−1}a\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},

δp′​(a)≡𝒬p′​(a)(modp).\delta^{\prime}_{p}(a)\equiv\mathcal{Q}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p}.

The proof is entirely analogous to the even case: one applies Lemma 4.1 to each polynomial Q⁡(x,k)Q(x,k) and then uses the definition of δp′​(a)\delta^{\prime}_{p}(a).

Theorem 4.5.

Let pp be an odd prime, and let a∈{0,…,p−1}a\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\} satisfy p|e2​a+1p\mid e_{2a+1}. If aa is a simple root of 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) modulo pp, then the odd internal branch Tp​(2​a+1)T_{p}(2a+1) is simple.

Proof.

Since aa is a simple root of 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) modulo pp, we have 𝒬p′​(a)≢0(modp)\mathcal{Q}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}. By Proposition 4.4, δp′​(a)≡𝒬p′​(a)≢0(modp)\delta^{\prime}_{p}(a)\equiv\mathcal{Q}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, and the conclusion follows from Theorem 2.4. ∎

Corollary 4.2.

If every root of 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) modulo pp is simple, then every odd internal branch of the valuation tree is simple.

The behavior at a multiple root is also parallel to the even case. Suppose that

B⁡(a)≡c​p(modp2)and𝒬p′​(a)≡0(modp).B(a)\equiv cp\pmod{p^{2}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{Q}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

By Proposition 4.4 and (2.9),

B⁡(a+j​p)p≡c(modp)\frac{B(a+jp)}{p}\equiv c\pmod{p}

for every j≥0j\geq 0. If c≢0(modp)c\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, then

νp​(e2​(a+j​p)+1)=1for every ​j≥0,\nu_{p}(e_{2(a+jp)+1})=1\qquad\text{for every }j\geq 0,

so the odd internal root 2​a+12a+1 is terminal. If c≡0(modp)c\equiv 0\pmod{p}, all pp children acquire a second factor of pp, and higher-order information is needed to distinguish them.

Finally, the odd polynomial satisfies the symmetry 𝒬p​(−x−1)=𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(-x-1)=\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x). Differentiating and evaluating at the fixed point a=(p−1)/2a=(p-1)/2 modulo pp gives

𝒬p′​(p−12)≡0(modp).\mathcal{Q}_{p}^{\prime}\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

Therefore, whenever the central odd index pp is an internal root, the corresponding root of 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) is necessarily multiple. This is precisely the phenomenon that occurs for p=3p=3.

4.3. A partial converse

The simple-root criterion gives a sufficient condition for an even internal branch to be simple. Under the additional assumption that the initial pp-adic valuation is exactly one, the converse also holds. Thus, in this case, simplicity of the branch is equivalent to both the nonvanishing of the Givens–Moll lifting parameter and the simplicity of the corresponding polynomial root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp.

Theorem 4.6.

Let pp be an odd prime, and let a∈{1,…,p−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\} satisfy νp​(e2​a)=1\nu_{p}(e_{2a})=1. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    the even internal branch Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) is simple;

  2. (2)

    δp​(a)≢0(modp)\delta_{p}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p};

  3. (3)

    aa is a simple root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp.

Proof.

The equivalence between (2) and (3) follows from Theorem 4.2, since

δp​(a)≡𝒫p′​(a)(modp),\delta_{p}(a)\equiv\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p},

and aa is already a root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp.

The implication (3)⇒(1)(3)\Rightarrow(1) is precisely Theorem 4.3.

It remains to prove (1)⇒(3)(1)\Rightarrow(3). Suppose that Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) is simple and that 𝒫p′​(a)≡0(modp)\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}. Since p∤ap\nmid a and e2​a=a​𝒫p​(a)e_{2a}=a\mathcal{P}_{p}(a), the assumption νp​(e2​a)=1\nu_{p}(e_{2a})=1 implies

𝒫p​(a)p≢0(modp).\frac{\mathcal{P}_{p}(a)}{p}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

By the multiple-root analysis above, this forces the root of Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a) to be terminal, contradicting the assumption that the branch is simple. Hence 𝒫p′​(a)≢0(modp)\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, so aa is a simple root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp. ∎

5. A recursive pp-adic lifting procedure

The results of the preceding section provide criteria for determining when an internal branch is simple. We now show that, for a simple branch, the lifting congruence can also be used recursively to follow its unique nonterminal vertex. We begin with the case p=13p=13, which illustrates the procedure and shows how the exact 1313-adic valuation of a term can be determined from a sequence of successively refined residue classes.

5.1. The case p=13p=13

We return to the case p=13p=13 considered earlier. Modulo 1313, the polynomial 𝒫13​(x)\mathcal{P}_{13}(x) factors as

𝒫13​(x)≡(x2−3)​(x2+3)​(x6+x4+5​x2−3)​(x14+6​x10+2​x6−5​x4−3​x2+1)(mod13).\mathcal{P}_{13}(x)\equiv{}(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}+3)(x^{6}+x^{4}+5x^{2}-3)(x^{14}+6x^{10}+2x^{6}-5x^{4}-3x^{2}+1)\pmod{13}.

The last two factors have no roots in 𝔽13\mathbb{F}_{13}. Moreover, the roots of x2−3x^{2}-3 are 44 and 99, while the roots of x2+3x^{2}+3 are 66 and 77. Hence the nonzero roots of 𝒫13​(x)\mathcal{P}_{13}(x) modulo 1313 are

4,6,7,9.4,\quad 6,\quad 7,\quad 9.

They correspond, respectively, to the even internal root vertices 88, 1212, 1414, and 1818, and hence to the internal branches

T13​(8),T13​(12),T13​(14),T13​(18).T_{13}(8),\quad T_{13}(12),\quad T_{13}(14),\quad T_{13}(18).

To determine the first surviving child of each branch, we use (4.4). Since A​(a)=𝒫13​(a)A(a)=\mathcal{P}_{13}(a) for 1≤a≤121\leq a\leq 12, set

ca≡𝒫13​(a)13(mod13),da≡𝒫13′​(a)(mod13).c_{a}\equiv\frac{\mathcal{P}_{13}(a)}{13}\pmod{13},\qquad d_{a}\equiv\mathcal{P}_{13}^{\prime}(a)\pmod{13}.

By (4.3), da≡δ13​(a)(mod13)d_{a}\equiv\delta_{13}(a)\pmod{13}. Thus the first surviving child is determined by the unique solution ja∈{0,…,12}j_{a}\in\{0,\ldots,12\} of

or equivalently,

ja≡−ca​da−1(mod13).j_{a}\equiv-c_{a}d_{a}^{-1}\pmod{13}.

Equation (4.1) yields the following data:

For instance, for a=4a=4, equation (4.4) becomes

8+5​j≡0(mod13).8+5j\equiv 0\pmod{13}.

Its unique solution is j=1j=1. Hence the surviving half-index modulo 13213^{2} is 4+13=174+13=17. Since the corresponding full index is twice the half-index, the first step of the branch is

8(mod26)⟶34(mod338).8\pmod{26}\longrightarrow 34\pmod{338}.

Applying the same calculation to the other three roots gives

12(mod26)\displaystyle 12\pmod{26} ⟶38(mod338),\displaystyle\longrightarrow 38\pmod{338},
14(mod26)\displaystyle 14\pmod{26} ⟶300(mod338),\displaystyle\longrightarrow 300\pmod{338},
18(mod26)\displaystyle 18\pmod{26} ⟶304(mod338).\displaystyle\longrightarrow 304\pmod{338}.

In each case, the remaining twelve children are terminal with valuation exactly 11.

The procedure can now be repeated at the unique surviving child. We illustrate this again for the branch rooted at 88. Its first surviving half-index is 1717. Since

A⁡(17)132≡8(mod13),\frac{A(17)}{13^{2}}\equiv 8\pmod{13},

and the slope along this branch is 𝒫13′​(4)≡5(mod13)\mathcal{P}_{13}^{\prime}(4)\equiv 5\pmod{13}, the next surviving digit is determined by

8+5​j≡0(mod13).8+5j\equiv 0\pmod{13}.

Thus j=1j=1, and the next surviving half-index is 17+132=18617+13^{2}=186. At the following step,

A⁡(186)133≡12(mod13),\frac{A(186)}{13^{3}}\equiv 12\pmod{13},

so the corresponding congruence is

12+5​j≡0(mod13).12+5j\equiv 0\pmod{13}.

Its unique solution is j=8j=8, giving the next surviving half-index 186+8⋅133=17762186+8\cdot 13^{3}=17762.

Therefore, in terms of the full index, the branch begins

8(mod26)⟶34(mod338)⟶372(mod4394)⟶35524(mod57122)⟶⋯.8\pmod{26}\longrightarrow 34\pmod{338}\longrightarrow 372\pmod{4394}\longrightarrow 35524\pmod{57122}\longrightarrow\cdots.

At each level, the surviving residue modulo 2⋅13r2\cdot 13^{r} splits into thirteen possible lifts modulo 2⋅13r+12\cdot 13^{r+1}, and the lifting congruence selects exactly one of them.

There are no odd internal branches for p=13p=13. Indeed, a direct computation shows that 𝒬13​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{13}(x) has no roots in 𝔽13\mathbb{F}_{13}. Hence, by (4.6), no odd residue class gives rise to an internal branch.

It remains to consider the distinguished even class. We have

𝒫13​(0)≡1(mod13).\mathcal{P}_{13}(0)\equiv 1\pmod{13}.

If 13|m13\mid m, then (2.5), with r=1r=1, gives

A⁡(13)=∑k=012P⁡(13,k)≡∑k=012P⁡(0,k)=𝒫13​(0)(mod13).A(13)=\sum_{k=0}^{12}P(13,k)\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{12}P(0,k)=\mathcal{P}_{13}(0)\pmod{13}.

Hence A⁡(m)≡1(mod13)A(m)\equiv 1\pmod{13}. Thus A⁡(m)A(m) is a 1313-adic unit, and since e2​m=m​A​(m)e_{2m}=mA(m), we obtain

ν13​(e2​m)=ν13​(m).\nu_{13}(e_{2m})=\nu_{13}(m).

Consequently, at level rr, the distinguished even class has the surviving residue 0(mod2⋅13r)0\pmod{2\cdot 13^{r}}.

The colored paths record the unique surviving full-index residue at each successive level, while the gray vertices represent terminal classes. For clarity, the distinguished even branch corresponding to the residue 00 is not displayed; as observed above, this branch survives independently at every level.

For example,

372≡8(mod26),372≡34(mod338),372≡372(mod4394),372\equiv 8\pmod{26},\qquad 372\equiv 34\pmod{338},\qquad 372\equiv 372\pmod{4394},

whereas 372∉ℛ4372\notin\mathcal{R}_{4}. Therefore

ν13​(e372)=3.\nu_{13}(e_{372})=3.

This example suggests a general procedure. Rather than constructing the entire valuation tree, one may follow only the unique surviving residue of each simple branch. We now formalize this lifting process.

5.2. The general lifting procedure

The preceding example suggests how to proceed for an arbitrary odd prime pp. Recall that

A⁡(m)=e2​mm,B⁡(m)=e2​m+1,A(m)=\frac{e_{2m}}{m},\qquad B(m)=e_{2m+1},

and define

Ep={a∈{1,…,p−1}:𝒫p​(a)≡0(modp)},E_{p}=\left\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\mathcal{P}_{p}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{p}\right\},

and

Op={b∈{0,…,p−1}:𝒬p​(b)≡0(modp)}.O_{p}=\left\{b\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}:\mathcal{Q}_{p}(b)\equiv 0\pmod{p}\right\}.

By the results of the preceding section, the elements of EpE_{p} correspond to the nonzero even internal branches Tp​(2​a)T_{p}(2a), while the elements of OpO_{p} correspond to the odd internal branches Tp​(2​b+1)T_{p}(2b+1). The distinguished even class 0(mod2​p)0\pmod{2p} will be treated separately.

We now describe how to follow the successive surviving residues of any simple branch.

Theorem 5.1.

Let pp be an odd prime. If a∈Epa\in E_{p} is a simple root of 𝒫p​(x)\mathcal{P}_{p}(x) modulo pp, then there exists a unique sequence

u1(a),u2(a),u3(a),…,0≤ur(a)<pr,u_{1}^{(a)},u_{2}^{(a)},u_{3}^{(a)},\ldots,\qquad 0\leq u_{r}^{(a)}<p^{r},

such that

u1(a)=a,ur+1(a)≡ur(a)(modpr),pr∣A(ur(a))u_{1}^{(a)}=a,\qquad u_{r+1}^{(a)}\equiv u_{r}^{(a)}\pmod{p^{r}},\qquad p^{r}\mid A\bigl(u_{r}^{(a)}\bigr)

for every r≥1r\geq 1.

Similarly, if b∈Opb\in O_{p} is a simple root of 𝒬p​(x)\mathcal{Q}_{p}(x) modulo pp, then there exists a unique sequence

v1(b),v2(b),v3(b),…,0≤vr(b)<pr,v_{1}^{(b)},v_{2}^{(b)},v_{3}^{(b)},\ldots,\qquad 0\leq v_{r}^{(b)}<p^{r},

such that

v1(b)=b,vr+1(b)≡vr(b)(modpr),pr∣B(vr(b))v_{1}^{(b)}=b,\qquad v_{r+1}^{(b)}\equiv v_{r}^{(b)}\pmod{p^{r}},\qquad p^{r}\mid B\bigl(v_{r}^{(b)}\bigr)

for every r≥1r\geq 1.

Proof.

We prove the even case; the odd case is analogous. Suppose that ur(a)u_{r}^{(a)} has been determined and set

cr(a)≡A⁡(ur(a))pr(modp).c_{r}^{(a)}\equiv\frac{A\bigl(u_{r}^{(a)}\bigr)}{p^{r}}\pmod{p}.

The pp possible lifts are ur(a)+j​pru_{r}^{(a)}+jp^{r}, for j=0,…,p−1j=0,\ldots,p-1. By (2.5),

A⁡(ur(a)+j​pr)pr≡cr(a)+j​δp​(ur(a))(modp).\frac{A\bigl(u_{r}^{(a)}+jp^{r}\bigr)}{p^{r}}\equiv c_{r}^{(a)}+j\delta_{p}\bigl(u_{r}^{(a)}\bigr)\pmod{p}.

Since ur(a)≡a(modp)u_{r}^{(a)}\equiv a\pmod{p}, Theorem 4.2 gives

δp​(ur(a))≡𝒫p′​(ur(a))≡𝒫p′​(a)(modp).\delta_{p}\bigl(u_{r}^{(a)}\bigr)\equiv\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}\bigl(u_{r}^{(a)}\bigr)\equiv\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p}.

Therefore

A⁡(ur(a)+j​pr)pr≡cr(a)+j​𝒫p′​(a)(modp).\frac{A\bigl(u_{r}^{(a)}+jp^{r}\bigr)}{p^{r}}\equiv c_{r}^{(a)}+j\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\pmod{p}.

Since 𝒫p′​(a)≢0(modp)\mathcal{P}_{p}^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}, there is a unique j∈{0,…,p−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\} for which the right-hand side vanishes. This determines the unique lift divisible by pr+1p^{r+1} and completes the recursion. ∎

The proof is constructive: once the surviving residue at a given level is known, the lifting congruence uniquely determines the next base-pp digit and, hence, the surviving residue at the next level. The odd case is entirely analogous. Consequently, along every simple branch, the exact pp-adic valuation of a term can be determined one base-pp digit at a time.
